Community-Led Sustainable Energy Projects and Community-Based Solutions
M3: Just Energy Transition
Lesson 2 Overview

Community-led sustainable energy projects serve as powerful tools for empowering local communities worldwide, exemplifying the transformative potential of grassroots initiatives in shaping a more just energy system.

These initiatives not only deploy renewable technologies and enhance <ai prompt="Provide more info on energy efficiency.">energy efficiency 💬️</ai> but also foster social cohesion, economic development, and environmental stewardship.

By prioritizing community engagement, these projects go beyond simply generating clean energy; they are about building trust and collaboration within communities while addressing historical societal inequalities in energy systems.
Real-world examples highlight the successes and lessons learned from community-led initiatives.

The RevoluSolar energy initiative in a brazilian favela brought renewable energy access to 30 families while reinvesting profits into local charities and job training programs, thereby improving overall citizen welfare and shielding residents from escalating energy costs.

The community of Magliano Alpi in the Italian Alps developed tools to forecast energy generation and demand, enabling effective utilization of solar photovoltaic systems and reducing reliance on the grid during peak demand periods.
The battery resource initiative in northern Perth, Australia, demonstrates how community-based energy projects can enhance collective savings and reduce grid stress.

Ongoing efforts to map similar initiatives and their benefits are being carried out under the IEA’s Digital Demand-Driven Electricity Networks Initiative (3DEN) as part of broader efforts to improve demand-side flexibility in clean energy transitions.
Policy support and regulatory reforms are essential for scaling up community-led energy projects and ensuring their widespread adoption.
Initiatives such as the European Parliament's funding for advisory services and technical assistance for community initiatives demonstrate steps in the right direction.

Additionally, sharing best practices globally can empower communities to access local, clean, and affordable energy solutions, thereby enhancing energy efficiency and community benefits through local generation and sharing, which can alleviate pressure on power systems and mitigate carbon emissions.

Case Study: Puerto Rico
Rebuilding energy sovereignty through community ownership –Cooperativa Hidroeléctrica de la Montaña pioneering solar-hydro resilience hubs and inter-municipal microgrids to empower communities.
ReEnFoCo–Resiliencia Energética Fotovoltaica Comunitaria (Community Photovoltaic Energy Resilience)

This initiative installs rooftop solar and battery systems on homes, businesses, and community centers, creating ‘resilience centers’ that maintain access to essential services during outages (Environmental and Energy Study Institute, 2020).
Hidroenergía Renace

Focused on the rehabilitation of the Caonillas and Dos Bocas hydroelectric plants, this initiative aims to restore up to 50 MW of renewable capacity and catalyze local economic development (Cooperativa Hidroelectrica de la Montana).
Microrred de la Montaña
The cooperative is designing Puerto Rico’s first inter-municipal microgrid, capable of operating in island mode and delivering reliable, distributed power across Adjuntas, Jayuya, Lares, and Utuado.
The cooperative initiated three key projects aimed at rebuilding local energy systems in a sustainable and inclusive manner.

The cooperative has faced several challenges along the way:
The rugged mountainous terrain of the project area posed engineering and logistical challenges for deploying solar, battery, and microgrid infrastructure.
Some stakeholders and community members expressed early skepticism about the feasibility of a cooperative-led energy model, which made transparency and visible results critical for building trust.

Securing financing for infrastructure restoration, particularly for hydroelectric rehabilitation, required significant time and effort and depended on collaboration with government and philanthropic partners
The cooperative had to navigate complex legal and regulatory frameworks, especially related to PREPA’s control over energy infrastructure and utility permitting processes.

Despite these hurdles, the cooperative’s transparent governance, strong local partnerships, and focus on mutual benefits helped to overcome these barriers.

These three projects represent a unified model of decentralized, community-owned energy transformation (Cooperativa Hidroeléctrica de la Montaña).

The phased implementation of the Cooperativa Hidroeléctrica de la Montaña has already begun to generate meaningful impacts across the central mountainous region of Puerto Rico.
Up to 250 rooftop systems, 10 MW solar, 20 MWh storage across 5 municipalities.
Rehabilitation of hydro plants to restore 50 MW capacity, benefiting ~40,000 homes

Puerto Rico’s first inter-municipal microgrid that integrates hydroelectric and solar generation, operates with islanding capability, and utilizes new 38 kV distribution lines between four municipalities.
Project serves ~90,000 residents in 4 municipalities.
Affordable, stable pricing; job creation through local workforce training
Strong political alliances and enabling policy frameworks were essential for overcoming regulatory and financial obstacles
The involvement of local knowledge and labor was indispensable in adapting technical solutions to the rugged terrain.
Rehabilitation of dormant infrastructure, such as the hydro plants, was both cost-effective and environmentally responsibles
The emphasis on community ownership is crucial in ensuring the project’s longevity and maintaining local resilience.
As a result of these efforts, the Cooperativa now operates across Adjuntas, Jayuya, Lares, and Utuado with the aim of increasing resilience, lowering energy burdens, and strengthening local capacity.

The cooperative also provides on-bill financing to improve affordability and energy access, especially for low-income households (EESI, 20234).

This project offers a model that can be replicated in other regions facing similar challenges, such as rural, mountainous, or disaster-prone areas with weak centralized energy access or abandoned infrastructure.
The key replicable elements include community-driven governance, the use of renewable energy sources, and leveraging local knowledge and labor.

These aspects ensure the project’s adaptability in other contexts, making it scalable and sustainable in regions with similar vulnerabilities.

The cooperative has established mechanisms to ensure the ongoing sustainability of the project.
Revenue generated from energy sales is reinvested into maintaining the energy systems and funding community development initiatives.

Moving forward, the cooperative plans to expand its microgrid coverage to additional towns, increase renewable energy generation capabilities to meet growing regional demand, and advocate for national policy reforms to support decentralized, community-based renewable energy systems across Puerto Rico.

By aligning with the principles of a <ai prompt="Tell me more about just energy transition.">just energy transition 💬️</ai>, this project not only enhances climate resilience but also advances social equity by empowering local communities to take charge of their energy futures.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Community-Led Energy Projects as Catalysts for Systemic Change

Community-led sustainable energy initiatives not only provide clean energy but also foster social cohesion, economic development, and environmental stewardship by empowering communities to own and manage their energy resources.
This approach shifts the paradigm from top-down energy systems to decentralized, participatory models that prioritize local needs and resilience.
Policy and Regulatory Frameworks are Key to Scaling Community Energy Solutions
The success of community-led energy projects hinges on supportive policy environments and regulatory reforms.
Initiatives like the European Parliament’s funding for advisory services and technical assistance highlight the importance of institutional backing.

By sharing best practices and providing financial and technical support, policymakers can enable the replication of successful models, ensuring that community energy projects can scale and thrive in diverse contexts.
Leveraging Existing Infrastructure for Sustainable Energy Transitions

Projects like the Microgrid of the Mountain in Puerto Rico illustrate the potential of repurposing underutilized infrastructure, such as old hydroelectric plants, to enhance energy resilience and sustainability.
This approach minimizes environmental impact and capital investment while maximizing local resource utilization.

By integrating local expertise and fostering collaborative governance, such initiatives can serve as blueprints for other regions seeking to optimize existing assets for community-driven energy solutions.
